sources.title: Paul Bettany (The Times interview by Tim Teeman, author repost)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, interviewed by Tim Teeman
sources.locator: Margin Call press interview; paragraphs on school, Matthew, cocaine, therapy, fame (author archive repost of The Times piece)
sources.excerpt: "I was a really bullied kid," ... "My godfather was gay and I would challenge every homophobic comment I heard. Consequently I had the shit kicked out of me because they thought I was gay." ... "It was a heart- breaking, alienating experience. I felt like I was harbouring this huge secret. I was so fragile." ... "I stopped because it was threatening my ability to act: the one thing that gave me self-worth." ... "God yes, four years on and off. In a world absent of Jesus, it's the flawed, but solitary option." ... He remains "full of self-doubt — I do not operate from a place of certainty". ... "But you shouldn't be sustained by other people's adulation. What if it goes away?" ... "I was terrified of reading aloud — it was so humil- iating that I used to hide." ... "I tot- ally fell in love with it the moment I started doing it."
sources.context: Long-form Times interview over lunch in New York, age 40, promoting Margin Call. Covers dyslexia and bullying, Matthew's death at 8 when Paul was 16, early-20s cocaine addiction ("work kept me on an even keel"), the 9/11 phone calls to Connelly, therapy, and fame. Teeman notes it is "all said without self-pity". Also: "Making Margin Call 'was the first amazing artistic experience I'd had in years' ... 'It made me think I can't be a gun for hire any more.'" Text read on the author's archive; the original Times page was not opened.

sources.title: Paul Bettany interview: this time it's serious (The Telegraph, Celia Walden)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, interviewed by Celia Walden
sources.locator: Full article via Wayback raw capture; paragraphs on lateness, son's birth and money, school bullying, 9/11, addiction, death
sources.excerpt: 'I have a pathological fear of being late' ... 'Suddenly I thought to myself, "---- all this. The world is precarious and I'm going to make my children as safe as possible – with dough." And I went about doing that. It was ludicrous, of course, because they were safe. ... but there I was hammering bits of wood against the window as though there were a zombie apocalypse coming. It sounds neurotic, but it's not, because the tap can turn off.' ... 'I was a city boy and I was terrified of everyone' ... 'My experience of addiction was very much linked to a lack of foundation, feeling rootless and not knowing who I was' ... 'I felt so uneducated. Those people were supersized to me and I was always trying to proximate the way they constructed their sentences.' ... 'I worry about death in general a lot.' ... 'It was constant,' ... 'I was bullied about everything, from the way I looked to the fact that my father had been a dancer.' ... 'I can tell you right now that I'm not feeling particularly guarded.' ... 'I thought to myself, "Why have I been calling this woman for three days?" Then suddenly it dawned on me.' ... Auditions 'were always fine, because I would never sight read, I would just learn things by heart. Right up until the read-through for A Beautiful Mind, I was still learning my lines by heart and pretending to read my part. Now I've stopped doing that. It was the anxiety that made my dyslexia worse.'
sources.context: Interview at the Chateau Marmont while shooting Transcendence, promoting Blood (2013). Walden reports he tries not to be away from family for longer than two weeks, that after 9/11 he rang Connelly for days ("Why have I been calling this woman for three days?"), and that the marriage gave him "a certainty that was new to me". She also reports his father "aged 75 ... announced his bisexuality", which conflicts with Bettany's later "came out at 63". The bullying at Chancellors school predates Matthew's death. Walden was warned he would not discuss his brother that day. Walden also reports the money plan included buying 'the 100-acre farm in Vermont he wanted his children to have as a weekend retreat', that his parents divorced in 1993, that he arrived 'two minutes late, having called to say he may be delayed', and that Master and Commander was 'a global box-office hit' in 2003. The 'It blew the family apart' line is quoted as something he 'has said'.

sources.title: Paul Bettany on How He Rekindled His Love for Acting (Daily Actor, relaying The Guardian)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, quoted from a Guardian interview
sources.locator: Second and third paragraphs quoting the Guardian Blood interview
sources.excerpt: "Acting used to be somewhere I could put loads of terrible feelings and bad experiences and try to make something creative out of them. But then I married and had children and everything got eclipsed. I know how precarious life can be, so I then had a period when I was making as much money as I could, so my children would be safe. Then I made a film called Margin Call, which was shot in two weeks on a low budget."
sources.context: Daily Actor summary of a 2013 Guardian interview about Blood. The Guardian original could not be opened (crawler blocked), so this is a secondary relay; the same safety-through-money account appears independently in S02 two weeks earlier and in S01.

sources.title: Interview: Paul Bettany On Creation (CinemaBlend)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany
sources.locator: Q&A answer on whether he was nervous acting with Connelly
sources.excerpt: My heartbeat tends to lower when cameras are on. I tend to get much calmer. I'm anxious in everyday life. I'm anxious about my kids' health, my health, whether I"m going to get the job I want, the chicken's going to turn out all right, the dog's going to poop in front of the paparazzi.
sources.context: Roundtable-style junket interview for Creation, in which he played Darwin opposite Connelly. sources.title: Paul Bettany on why his directorial debut is about homelessness (The Independent, Kaleem Aftab)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, interviewed by Kaleem Aftab
sources.locator: Paragraphs on the film's theme, busking, and his father
sources.excerpt: "But I didn't want to make a film about homelessness," he insists. "I wanted it to be about judgment." ... "It's just that people are eminently forgivable." ... "My father, who has just died, was a very religious man," says Bettany. "I'm not. I was raised a Catholic and he used to say this thing whenever we passed a homeless person, 'There but for the grace of God, go I.' Although I'm not a religious man, I love that sentence. There is an admission of how easily it can be us."
sources.context: Interview about Shelter (2014), which he wrote and directed and which stars Connelly. The story was inspired by a homeless couple outside his New York home. He says his busking past probably fed the film but "I didn't want it to become part of a narrative in discussing the film". Connelly, he says, "is incredibly honest about my artistic endeavours – brutally so."

sources.title: Paul Bettany talks 'Uncle Frank' and his own closeted father (Windy City Times)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany
sources.locator: Q&A answer to whether he was reluctant to accept the role
sources.excerpt: But the first question I had for Alan was "Why me?," and I [followed that] with "Should I even do this?" ... My father, because of the dogma of Catholicism, went back into the closet. He was arguably with the love of his life and when my father died—in my arms!—I found in his pocket a glass vial of Andy's ashes. ... My father had some beautifully curated stories and anecdotes, but I never really got to know him because he didn't live his life in an authentic way.
sources.context: Phone Q&A for Uncle Frank (2020), in which he plays a closeted gay professor. He says he asked himself whether it was "morally correct" to take the role and whether he had "the energy" to "think of some dark moments in your life". He and director Alan Ball found they shared "early traumas in our lives and deaths of our siblings".

sources.title: Exclusive Interview: Paul Bettany ... shares a touching story about his father coming out late in life (The Queer Review)

sources.title: Paul Bettany Says His Gay Father Went Back Into The Closet in His 80s (Out, relaying Total Film and NewNowNext)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany (via Total Film); Alan Ball (via NewNowNext)

We could of course try the English course of action in these predicaments — we do a drowning test. Thoughts?" ... "We live in a world without context," he said. sources.title: Paul Bettany on fame, playing the game, and staying sane (Gentleman's Journal, Joseph Bullmore)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, interviewed by Joseph Bullmore
sources.locator: Hour-long Zoom interview; sections on emotion access, fame, isolation, "Finish strong", neurosis
sources.excerpt: "Some people have amazing access to their emotions, and can switch them on like that," ... "And I'm just not good enough to do that." ... "if I find myself in a scene that requires that, I find myself picking at scabs that I'd rather not pick at," ... "But it's spurious and I have watched it, with myself, come and go — it's an untrustworthy thing. You shouldn't find solace in it." ... "You're certainly not meeting the actual me, and I'm not meeting who you really are." ... "What I have realised is that I do better than I think in isolation," he says. "I'm quite convivial and social, and so I'm always surprised to see how well I do with my own company. I feel like I shouldn't have the personal resources to be on my own at all. I feel like I should fall apart more than I do. But I don't." ... "It's irritatingly industrious of me. But I have that ethos myself, when I'm up at work and tired and against it." ... "I'm not any less neurotic now, by the way" he says before we go. "I'm just better at hiding it." ... "you've only ever seen this really carefully curated public persona" ... "And it's like: What am I doing? What am I doing! What the hell am I doing! Sat here in front of a graveyard, thinking about dead people in my life?" ... "That's something that makes me feel less alone and alienated in the world" ... "I'm quite convivial and social, and so I'm always surprised to see how well I do with my own company. I feel like I shouldn't have the personal resources to be on my own at all."
sources.context: Interview from a cabin near his Vermont house for the film of The Collaboration. Also: Talking about acting "is like talking about sex"; the Lennon lyric "makes me feel less alone and alienated in the world"; a fan asked for a selfie while he stood crying after hearing his father was gravely ill. The journalist calls Stellan "the oldest" of the children; Kai, Connelly's son, is older. The 'less alone and alienated' line is about John Lennon's lyric from 'Mother', which the writer calls the most moving lyric Bettany can think of. The Warhol line describes why he first refused the role. The sweatshirt detail is the writer's report of what Bettany 'has said in interviews before'.

sources.title: Paul Bettany on playing Warhol, family ghosts, and how therapy 'saved' him (The Daily Beast, Tim Teeman, author repost)
sources.speaker: Paul Bettany, interviewed by Tim Teeman
sources.locator: Zoom interview during the Broadway run of The Collaboration; sections on fear, bullying, father, therapy, work ethic, career slump, Depp, citizenship
sources.excerpt: "For instance, with Andy Warhol, it's his fear. I was very bullied as a schoolkid, and I remember the world feeling like a frightening place. I try to remember that in me." ... "I wouldn't take part in any of the homophobic banter around me, and the consequence of that, well you can imagine… I sort of refused to bend on that." ... "It's more that I have a really strong work ethic. ... The thing I could control was being the most prepared person auditioning that day." ... "I couldn't just fall apart. What was making me feel safe and relevant was my career, rather like Warhol. Then my children came along, and all of that disappeared like mist." ... "We had kids, suddenly we had a fucking mortgage. I thought, what if this thing comes tumbling down?" ... "I said to him, 'Look, this town is full of second and third acts, and you should mind your fucking manners.' I walked out. My legs went because I acted so tough!" ... "When I'm away from them too much I begin to revert to older habits," ... "I am so much less certain and definitive about things." ... "I refuse to put more fuel on this fire that's just been really unpleasant." ... "It's more that I have a really strong work ethic." ... "He said, 'Well that was only physical for a very short time.'" ... "While I understand therapy is like having a chronic injury where you need to constantly be doing physical therapy and massage or you lean back into old patterns of behavior, I have also discovered it has really saved me." ... "My father had been a dancer and actor."
sources.context: Daily Beast interview reposted on the author's site. Also: therapy "absolutely saved me" and is "like having a chronic injury" needing upkeep or "you lean back into old patterns"; "I was very lost for a number of years, but there were always something that saved me or people that saved me"; politics occupies him "to an unhealthy extent"; he took US citizenship because he "was tired of getting shouted down on Twitter for having an opinion". Teeman reports the father died "aged 86 in 2015" and Bettany says his father came out "when he was 63". Bettany declined to discuss the Depp texts further. Teeman reports Thane became 'a first-time father at 42'. The 'safe and relevant' line refers to his career before his children arrived ('Then my children came along, and all of that disappeared like mist'), not to the post-2008 slump; the draft does not use it.

sources.title: Paul Bettany explores being art star Andy Warhol on Broadway (AP, Mark Kennedy, via KTVZ)

I was being painted as this close friend of a guy I hadn't spoken to in years and, honestly, amid all the s--- two celebrities threw at each other, that bit was the most odd," he said. sources.context: Sibling Revelry episode released 13 October 2026, the day before VisionQuest premiered; hosts Kate and Oliver Hudson, Bettany speaking from New York. Audio downloaded from the public RSS enclosure and transcribed locally (whisper small.en for the whole episode; the quoted clips re-transcribed with large-v3-turbo, which agreed). The conversation has three voices and no speaker labels, so only lines that answer a question put to Bettany are attributed; nearby remarks about actors needing approval and validation are not attributed to him. Both models heard "couldn't turn very negative things into something creative" where the sense suggests "could"; that phrase is not quoted. The 9/11 account here says "about 48 hours" of calling; the 2013 Telegraph has "three days". He attributes the lyric "Mother, you had me, but I never had you" to "Sean Lennon"; it is John Lennon's "Mother". He says his father came out "at 63", consistent with his 2020 and 2022 accounts. Draft stage (2026-10-30): the clips for career worry, safety net, punctuality, the mask answer and 9/11 were transcribed a third time with whisper medium.en. Quoted spans are words all three models share, or (for 'being on time' and 'second string to your bow') two of three where the third is a clear mishearing ('one time', 'bone'); the bow phrase is paraphrased, not quoted. Quotations drop spoken false starts and stutters ('I can do, I can do', 'the, the trauma and, and, and drama'). Small.en and turbo disagree on 'which bits were me' / 'which bits for me' (medium: 'were me'), so that clause is paraphrased. These are machine transcriptions, not a human listen.

claims.claim: Bettany's younger brother Matthew died at age 8 after falling from a tennis pavilion roof at the school where their father taught; Paul was 16, and he says the death "blew the family apart".
claims.passage: Then, when he was 16, his eight-year-old brother Matthew fell from the roof of a tennis pavilion and died.
claims.inference: A dated, repeatedly told formative loss; it establishes the circumstance every later safety-seeking choice has to be weighed against.
claims.alternative: Grief and trauma alone can produce lifelong hypervigilance in any type; this event cannot by itself show type.

claims.claim: In October 2026 he said Matthew fell from a building "that I had taught him how to climb", leaving "an enormous amount of guilt to work through".
claims.passage: Matthew "fell off a building that I had taught him how to climb. So there was an enormous amount of guilt to work through on that."
claims.inference: Adds a self-blame strand that later interviews show being worked through in therapy; useful as a late, specific disclosure rather than as type proof.
claims.alternative: Survivor guilt after a sibling death is common and circumstantial; it does not discriminate between 6 and 4.

claims.claim: He describes fear as predating the brother's death: bullied constantly at his Hertfordshire school, he says "I was a city boy and I was terrified of everyone".
claims.passage: "I was a city boy and I was terrified of everyone," Bettany told the Telegraph. The bullying at his Hertfordshire school, he said, was "constant," and it covered "everything, from the way I looked to the fact that my father had been a dancer."
claims.inference: Fearfulness reported before the 16-year-old's trauma weakens a trauma-only explanation of his later vigilance and supports an anxious baseline.
claims.alternative: Bullying is itself a circumstance; the fear may be situational to that school rather than temperamental.

claims.claim: At school he refused to join homophobic banter and challenged it, and was beaten for it; he says "I sort of refused to bend on that."
claims.passage: His godfather was gay, and he challenged the homophobic talk around him. "Consequently I had the shit kicked out of me because they thought I was gay,"
claims.inference: Taking a costly stand for a threatened in-group (his gay godfather, father's world) fits a loyal, counterphobic Six pattern of standing firm against the threat.
claims.alternative: Could equally reflect Four identification with outsiders, or simple moral conviction; it does not by itself discriminate.

claims.claim: In his early twenties he became addicted to cocaine, which he linked to "a lack of foundation, feeling rootless and not knowing who I was".
claims.passage: "My experience of addiction was very much linked to a lack of foundation, feeling rootless and not knowing who I was."
claims.inference: His own diagnosis of the addiction is about missing foundation, i.e. security and grounding.
claims.alternative: "Not knowing who I was" is also classic Four identity language; this passage cuts both ways.

claims.claim: He says he quit cocaine because it threatened his ability to act, "the one thing that gave me self-worth".
claims.passage: He quit, he told The Times, "because it was threatening my ability to act: the one thing that gave me self-worth."
claims.inference: Work functioned as a stabilising structure; he chose the structure over the drug.
claims.alternative: A Three reading (worth through work) also fits this line; the later rejection of praise as a measure (C12) weighs against that.

claims.claim: After the 9/11 calls he married Connelly on 1 January 2003 in Scotland without having lived together first; he said the marriage gave him "a certainty that was new to me".
claims.passage: They married in Scotland on January 1, 2003, without having lived together first. The marriage, he told the Telegraph, gave him "a certainty that was new to me."
claims.inference: A threat to someone he cared about produced checking behaviour and then a commitment that he describes in terms of certainty: a security move.
claims.alternative: Crisis-driven romantic clarity is common in many types; the "certainty" phrase is a journalist's paraphrase-adjacent quote from one interview.

claims.claim: When his son was born he decided "the world is precarious" and set out to make his children "as safe as possible – with dough", taking studio jobs for money; he called it "hammering bits of wood against the window as though there were a zombie apocalypse coming".
claims.passage: It was ludicrous, of course, because they were safe. My wife and I make enough money to ensure their safety, but there I was hammering bits of wood against the window as though there were a zombie apocalypse coming. It sounds neurotic, but it's not, because the tap can turn off.
claims.inference: The clearest repeated, costly choice: he traded artistic preference for financial security, while recognising the threat was exaggerated. This is the main Six discriminator against Four.
claims.alternative: Ordinary parental prudence, and an actor's incentive to justify commercial roles in hindsight; a Four could make the same trade under pressure.

claims.claim: After making Margin Call (2011) cheaply, he said "I can't be a gun for hire any more" and that the film reminded him what he loved about acting.
claims.passage: Making it, he told The Times, "was the first amazing artistic experience I'd had in years," and "It made me think I can't be a gun for hire any more."
claims.inference: Shows the security strategy was revisable once a safer footing existed; meaning returned after safety.
claims.alternative: This return to artistic meaning is the strongest Four-compatible turn in the record.

claims.claim: He frames his professional discipline as control over uncertainty: "I have a really strong work ethic" and "The thing I could control was being the most prepared person auditioning that day."
claims.passage: The thing I could control was being the most prepared person auditioning that day.
claims.inference: Preparation as a hedge against what cannot be controlled, repeated across 2013, 2022 and 2026.
claims.alternative: Professional craft norms and British punctuality; Olsen's "precise" remark could reflect training rather than anxiety.

claims.claim: He describes himself as anxious in everyday life but calmer once cameras roll (2010).
claims.passage: My heartbeat tends to lower when cameras are on. I tend to get much calmer. I'm anxious in everyday life.
claims.inference: Consistent first-person anxiety across 2010, 2012 and 2022, including the observation that he becomes calmer once the camera (action) starts.
claims.alternative: Self-deprecating anxiety talk is also a British comic register and a junket habit; self-report cannot show the motive is core.

claims.claim: He treats fame and praise as unreliable supports: "What if it goes away?" (2012); "it's an untrustworthy thing. You shouldn't find solace in it" (2022); judging yourself by others' praise is one of the "terrible, terrible things" about the job.
claims.passage: In 2012 he told The Times that "you shouldn't be sustained by other people's adulation. What if it goes away?" A decade later fame was "an untrustworthy thing. You shouldn't find solace in it"
claims.inference: Distrust of an external support, framed as a security question, argues against a Three reading and fits Six scepticism.
claims.alternative: A Four also distrusts fame because it misrecognises the "actual me" (C18).

claims.claim: He says he worries about death "a lot" (2013).
claims.passage: "I worry about death in general a lot," he told the Telegraph.
claims.inference: Threat-scanning focused on the safety of loved ones, consistent with a Six attention pattern.
claims.alternative: Directly traceable to Matthew's fall; circumstance may explain it fully. The Telegraph writer's sense that it might exist even without the loss is impression, not evidence.

claims.claim: After the 2008 crash he made films that "helped us financially", worried "what if this thing comes tumbling down?", and then could not get a job for about two years.
claims.passage: he made films that "helped us financially. We had kids, suddenly we had a fucking mortgage. I thought, what if this thing comes tumbling down? For around two years I couldn't get a job."
claims.inference: Explicit safety language attached to work and money, a decade after C08.
claims.alternative: Financial worry after 2008 was widespread and circumstantial.

claims.claim: When a producer told him his career was over, he says he answered "you should mind your fucking manners", walked out, and his legs gave way because "I acted so tough"; minutes later Joss Whedon called offering Vision. Later tellings vary in detail.
claims.passage: In the 2022 version, Bettany answered, "Look, this town is full of second and third acts, and you should mind your fucking manners." Then: "I walked out. My legs went because I acted so tough!"
claims.inference: Bravado in the face of a threat followed by collapse is the counterphobic Six sequence in miniature; he tells it against himself.
claims.alternative: A polished, much-repeated anecdote shaped for audiences; details shift between versions (middle finger, sitting on the pavement), so treat it as self-mythology with a stable core.

claims.claim: He has been in therapy for years ("a thousand years" by 2021-2022) and compares it to treating a chronic injury so you do not "lean back into old patterns of behavior".
claims.passage: and treats it as maintenance, "like having a chronic injury" that needs constant work or "you lean back into old patterns of behavior."
claims.inference: Long reliance on a trusted support structure and maintenance mindset.
claims.alternative: Therapy use is common across types and among actors; it shows self-work, not type.

claims.claim: He says family keeps him steady: "When I'm away from them too much I begin to revert to older habits."
claims.passage: "When I'm away from them too much I begin to revert to older habits," he told the Daily Beast of his family.
claims.inference: Family as the secure base that regulates him, repeated 2013-2026.
claims.alternative: Devoted-parent statements are standard press fare and fit many types.

claims.claim: He speaks in Four-like terms of alienation: fans are "not meeting the actual me"; he counts himself among "the weirdos".
claims.passage: Fans who pose with him, he said, are "certainly not meeting the actual me." And in 2026 he told Square Mile that _WandaVision_ was made "for the weirdos. I count myself as one of them."
claims.inference: This is the strongest evidence for the Four alternative and must be shown honestly.
claims.alternative: The alienation passages describe grief and fame encounters, not a cultivated identity of difference; elsewhere he deflates his own artistic self-image (C19).

claims.claim: He deflates his own artistry: others access emotion more easily "And I'm just not good enough to do that"; he is "quite lazy" about playing a robot.
claims.passage: Some actors switch on emotion easily, he said, "And I'm just not good enough to do that." He calls himself "quite lazy" about playing a robot because the costume and prosthetics do the work
claims.inference: A Four typically invests in the artist-self and its emotional depth; Bettany treats his own as faintly embarrassing and frames emotion access as a technique he must work at.
claims.alternative: Could be British self-deprecation or junket modesty rather than motive.

claims.claim: To cry on camera he describes "picking at scabs that I'd rather not pick at"; Gentleman's Journal reports he kept Matthew's sweatshirt on set for Uncle Frank.
claims.passage: "I find myself picking at scabs that I'd rather not pick at," and the magazine reported he kept Matthew's sweatshirt with him on set for a graveyard scene in _Uncle Frank_.
claims.inference: Shows he uses grief deliberately as a work tool and then questions it ("What the hell am I doing!").
claims.alternative: Using personal pain in art is a Four-compatible behaviour; the method framing is also standard actor training (Drama Centre London).

claims.claim: By Bettany's account his father Thane came out at 63 and spent about 20 years with Andy Clark, "a joyous relief for everybody".
claims.passage: By his son's account he came out at 63, then spent about 20 years with a man named Andy Clark. "It was a joyous relief for everybody, actually," Bettany told Total Film in 2020,
claims.inference: A father who lived inauthentically for safety is a central family story and the background to his Uncle Frank, Warhol and VisionQuest comments.
claims.alternative: Dates conflict: Telegraph 2013 says Thane announced bisexuality "aged 75". Use Bettany's own account, attributed, and avoid exact ages beyond what he says.

claims.claim: From his father's retreat into the closet he drew a parenting rule: "I really want my children ... to just live authentically as the person they are".
claims.passage: I really want my children, and I want everybody, to just live authentically as the person they are
claims.inference: Value statement; supports the Four alternative's authenticity theme and also a Six-style protective vow for the next generation.
claims.alternative: Parenting values statements in People magazine are low-cost signals.

claims.claim: He hesitated over Uncle Frank, asking "Why me?" and "Should I even do this?"; director Alan Ball said the film became Paul's "what if" story about his father.
claims.passage: Bettany's first questions were "Why me?" and "Should I even do this?" Ball later said that "for Paul, the movie became a chance for him to have his own 'what if' story about his father" (NewNowNext, relayed by Out).
claims.inference: Doubt-first engagement with an offer, then commitment once a reason is found; Ball's testimony places the motive in repairing the father story.
claims.alternative: The hesitation is partly the 2020 debate about straight actors in gay roles, which he names.

claims.claim: In October 2026 he told The Times he "decided to say nothing" about the Depp texts, though he had commented on them in 2021 and 2022.
claims.passage: He added that he "decided to say nothing because, I think, people know me." He had in fact commented in 2021 and 2022.
claims.inference: Threat-anticipating caution about public speech, plus a small contradiction between "say nothing" and his earlier comments.
claims.alternative: Normal crisis-PR caution for any celebrity; the contradiction may be compression by the 2026 interviewer.
claims.review_trigger: New statements by Bettany, Depp or Heard about the texts; any change in the 2026 VisionQuest boycott story; publication of the full Times 2026 interview.

claims.claim: In 2013 text messages read in Depp's 2020 UK libel case, Bettany replied to Depp's "Let's burn Amber!!!" by joking that they should instead do "a drowning test"; in 2016 he tweeted that Depp was "the sweetest, kindest, gentlest man"; since 2022 he has said they had not spoken for years and in 2026 that they have not spoken since.
claims.passage: Bettany replied, as [Insider](https://news.yahoo.com/paul-bettany-says-embarrassing-texts-111303945.html) printed it, "Having thought it through I don't think we should burn Amber — she's delightful company and easy on the eye, plus I'm not sure she's a witch. We could of course try the English course of action in these predicaments — we do a drowning test. Thoughts?"
claims.inference: A documented episode that shows loyalty to a friend in 2016 and later distancing; relevant to how he handles allegiance and threat.
claims.alternative: Sensitive: the texts concern a woman who alleged abuse, and Depp has denied abuse. Describe neutrally, attribute exact words, avoid motive claims, and note that court outcomes differed (UK 2020 loss; US 2022 jury largely for Depp; 2022 settlement).
claims.review_trigger: Any new court filing, statement or reporting on the Bettany-Depp texts or friendship; reassess before refresh.

claims.claim: He has lived in the US longer than he lived in England and took US citizenship.
claims.passage: who has lived in the United States for more than two decades and took US citizenship
claims.inference: Biographical metadata only.
claims.alternative: The date of naturalisation is not established; the draft gives none.

claims.claim: He calls himself "quite convivial and social" and is surprised he copes alone.
claims.passage: but he calls himself "quite convivial and social" and says, "I feel like I shouldn't have the personal resources to be on my own at all."
claims.inference: Sociability and surprise at self-sufficiency weigh against a Five reading; may suggest a Seven-leaning Six.
claims.alternative: A Seven or a Nine reading leans on this register; his sustained attention to death and threat weighs against Seven.

claims.claim: Elizabeth Olsen: "He's very precise, like me."
claims.passage: "He's very precise, like me," Elizabeth Olsen told Grazia
claims.inference: Independent named testimony on work habits that is consistent with his own preparation account.
claims.alternative: Thin, promotional testimony about craft; it says nothing direct about motive.

claims.claim: Born in London in 1971; voices J.A.R.V.I.S. and plays Vision; Emmy-nominated for WandaVision.
claims.passage: Bettany, born in London in 1971, is the voice of J.A.R.V.I.S. and the face of Vision in Marvel's films, an Emmy nominee for _WandaVision_
claims.inference: Metadata scaffolding only.
claims.alternative: Children's ages change; avoid ages in the article.

claims.claim: VisionQuest began streaming on Disney+ on 14 October 2026.
claims.passage: which began streaming on Disney+ on October 14, 2026
claims.inference: Current hook that rhymes with the father story; it should date, not carry, the argument.
claims.alternative: Promotional framing; do not claim Avengers: Doomsday or Secret Wars appearances, which are unconfirmed.
claims.review_trigger: VisionQuest finale and any renewal or cancellation news; official confirmation or denial of Bettany in Avengers: Doomsday (18 December 2026) or Secret Wars (2027).

claims.claim: Bettany says Marvel let him turn down work, spend time with family, direct, and get films funded, and that the Vision call came minutes after he was told his career was over.
claims.passage: "It means I have been able to not take jobs and spend time with my family," he told Reuters.
claims.inference: The franchise became a security floor, which fits the family-first, safety-first pattern.
claims.alternative: Many actors credit franchises with financial freedom; not discriminating.
claims.review_trigger: Future statements about leaving or continuing as Vision.

claims.claim: He says acting and drama school saved him because "there was always a mask that I could hide behind", so nobody knew which parts were him.
claims.passage: Drama school saved him, he went on, because "there was always a mask that I could hide behind,"
claims.inference: A Four typically wants the true self seen and expressed; Bettany chose the art form that conceals him and framed it as a fallback for safety. This is the clearest single discriminator against the Four alternative.
claims.alternative: Ordinary stage fright about one's own songs; or Five-style privacy. He still used the work to process grief, which a Four reading can claim.

claims.claim: He calls himself "an absolute fascist about being on time", traces the habit to drama-school theatre discipline ("always building more time to be there"), and repeats Anthony Hopkins's "If you're five minutes early, you're late."
claims.passage: "I have a pathological fear of being late," he said. Thirteen years later he called himself "an absolute fascist about being on time"
claims.inference: A thirteen-year consistent habit ("pathological fear of being late" in 2013) that functions as a buffer against things going wrong.
claims.alternative: Professional training and personal style; a One would also be strict about time, though nothing else in the record suggests a One's moral perfectionism.

claims.claim: Asked in 2026 whether the fear that each job is his last ever ends, he said "I don't think that ever ends, no. Which is really depressing," and that after a couple of months off he wonders "if anybody remembers me".
claims.passage: he said he doesn't think "that ever ends," then added, "which is really depressing." After a couple of months off, he said, he starts to think, "I wonder if anybody remembers me."
claims.inference: Continuing work insecurity at 55, after franchise success, fits the security pattern in C08 and C14.
claims.alternative: A Three reading (needing to be seen) or ordinary actor insecurity; the hosts said they feel the same.

claims.claim: Bettany believes his father returned to the closet because he "had to get into heaven as a straight man so he could see his son who had died".
claims.passage: Thane "had to get into heaven as a straight man so he could see his son who had died." That is Bettany's interpretation.
claims.inference: Bettany's own reading of his father's motive ties the family's two great losses together; it is his interpretation, not established fact about Thane Bettany's mind.
claims.alternative: Thane Bettany's own reasons are not on record; attribute the interpretation to Paul.

claims.claim: He memorised scripts to avoid sight-reading at auditions until A Beautiful Mind and says anxiety made his dyslexia worse.
claims.passage: "Right up until the read-through for A Beautiful Mind, I was still learning my lines by heart and pretending to read my part," he told the Telegraph in 2013.
claims.inference: Preparation began as concealment of a perceived weakness, consistent with the preparation pattern (C10).
claims.alternative: Ordinary coping with undiagnosed dyslexia; not type-specific.

claims.claim: After Matthew's death he saw "the fragility and the precariousness of your own position" and felt "totally alienated from all of your friends".
claims.passage: Not only do you lose that immediately and see the fragility and the precariousness of your own position
claims.inference: In context the "dreadful secret" is knowledge of precariousness, a security theme.
claims.alternative: Secondary relay of a 2012 Guardian interview (original not opened). The alienation half is the Four alternative's strongest line.

claims.claim: In 2013 he said acting had been where he put "terrible feelings" until marriage and children "eclipsed" it and he made as much money as he could so his children would be safe.
claims.passage: Acting used to be somewhere I could put loads of terrible feelings and bad experiences and try to make something creative out of them.
claims.inference: When expression and safety competed, he reports choosing safety; the main Six discriminator.
claims.alternative: Secondary relay of the Guardian (original not opened); the same account appears in S02. Hindsight justification of commercial work is possible.

claims.claim: Depp denies abusing Heard; he told the court the texts were a Monty Python riff; a 2022 Virginia jury largely sided with Depp and found for Heard on one counterclaim; they settled in December 2022.
claims.passage: Depp told the court the exchange was a riff on Monty Python, never meant literally. In his 2022 US defamation trial against Heard, a Virginia jury largely sided with Depp and found for Heard on one of her counterclaims, and the two settled in December 2022.
claims.inference: Neutral legal context for the texts.
claims.alternative: Court outcomes are reported via secondary outlets; the trial in which Depp gave the Monty Python testimony is not specified by the source.
claims.review_trigger: New court filings or reporting on Depp v. Heard or the Bettany texts.

claims.claim: In October 2026 some social media users called for a VisionQuest boycott over the texts.
claims.passage: with some social media users [calling for a _VisionQuest_ boycott](https://www.comicbasics.com/paul-bettany-breaks-his-silence-on-johnny-depp-texts-as-visionquest-faces-boycott-calls/) over the texts
claims.inference: Explains renewed 2026 attention.
claims.alternative: Scale of the boycott calls is not measured.
claims.review_trigger: Any change in the VisionQuest boycott story.

claims.claim: On 9/11 he spent about 48 hours (2026 telling) or three days (2013 telling) phoning Connelly before realising he loved her.
claims.passage: that he spent "no word of a lie, about 48 hours trying to ring Jennifer."
claims.inference: Threat to someone he cared about produced repeated checking, then commitment.

type_hypothesis.against: The Four case is real. Bettany speaks of alienation after Matthew's death ("harbouring some dreadful secret about what life is actually like"), of fans "not meeting the actual me", of himself as one of "the weirdos", and of authenticity as the lesson of his father's life. He mines his grief for performances with talismans, says acting was where he put "terrible feelings", and returned to artistic meaning after Margin Call. His anxiety and death preoccupation can also be explained by circumstance alone: a sibling's fatal fall at 16, school bullying, addiction and a precarious freelance trade, so some of the Six signal may be trauma rather than type. Much of the record is promotional interviews, where self-deprecating worry is also a British comic register. The 2026 podcast answer that calls acting a mask also says "I can do something with this brokenness that I am feeling" (C58), the Four reading's best single line.
type_hypothesis.alternative_case: Type 4: a man shaped by loss who feels set apart from people who have not seen "what life is actually like", who uses acting as a container for painful feeling, who keeps returning to stories of men who could not live as themselves (Uncle Frank, Warhol, a Vision with memories he cannot feel), and who prizes authenticity above safety after watching his father retreat into the closet. Margin Call's rescue of his love for acting, the scab-picking method and the "actual me" remark all fit.
type_hypothesis.discriminator: What he does when the floor drops away. A Four turns toward the loss to deepen a distinct identity; a Six moves to secure the base and pre-empt the next threat. Across 2010-2026 Bettany repeatedly does the second, at a cost: after 9/11 he phones for two or three days, then commits, and calls marriage "a certainty that was new to me" (2013); at his son's birth he decides "The world is precarious" and sets out to make the children safe "with dough", knowing it was ludicrous (2013), and says acting as a place for "terrible feelings" was "eclipsed" by that safety plan (2013 Guardian relay); after 2008 he asks "what if this thing comes tumbling down?" (2022); he copes with uncertainty by being "the most prepared person" and never late (2013, 2022, 2026); he distrusts fame because "What if it goes away?" (2012) and it is "untrustworthy" (2022). His fearfulness predates the brother's death ("terrified of everyone" as a bullied city boy), and the 'dreadful secret' he describes after it is "the precariousness of your own position". The sharpest single test is how he chose his art form: he gave up songwriting because he hated singing his own songs in front of people and felt "so revealed", called acting his "safety net", says drama school saved him because "there was always a mask that I could hide behind", and is "not sure I want anybody to really know that much about me definitively" (2026). He also does not want to "trade on the trauma and drama of it all". He deflates rather than cultivates his artist-self ("sounding like a ponce", "I'm just not good enough", "quite lazy").
type_hypothesis.unexplained: He deliberately reopens grief for work and has played a run of men hiding their true selves, which the Six reading explains only as craft, not as choice. He is candid to the point of oversharing in interviews despite saying he is cautious, and his convivial, joking register (and early cocaine use) is more Seven-flavoured than the anxious core suggests. His 2016 public praise of Depp versus his later account of years without contact is not fully reconciled. The wish not to be known "definitively" could also be read as Five-style privacy, though his sociability and reliance on people and therapy argue against Five. Some 2026 podcast lines about actors never feeling fulfilled are hard to attribute to a speaker from audio alone and are not used. Wing is not established; sociability suggests 6w7 but this is optional and unproven.
